newsitem.title: USA: Clinton urged to get tough with party on reform.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urged to get tough with party on reform.

text.p: A former Democratic Party chairman urged President Clinton Thursday to get tough and withhold support from Democratic congressional candidates unless they commit themselves to campaign reform.

Unless Clinton uses leverage with his own party members, chances are dim for passage of serious campaign reform in Congress by Clinton's goal of July 4, Paul Kirk, who served as Democratic chairman between 1985 and 1989, said in a speech prepared for delivery at George Washington University.

Clinton has backed a plan for voluntary spending limits in return for free television air time along with restrictions on raising campaign funds. But there is little support in Congress for major reforms since incumbents are the major beneficiaries of the current system.

"The president has been accused by some as appearing disingenuous in calling for campaign reform on the one hand while actively raising new campaign funds on the other," Boston lawyer Kirk said. "In my view, with less than 50 legislative days left until his July 4 target, it is time for the president to take a 'tough love' approach with Democratic congressional candidates."

This was the first major speech on campaign reform by a former chairman of either party, Kirk noted. In his speech, he delivered a harsh indictment on the role of money in politics, currently the focus of federal investigations into improper money-raising involving Clinton's White House and party.

Noting that a record amount was spent in the 1996 election, Kirk bemoaned the fact that voter turnout was the lowest of any democracy in the world. "In the most free and most advanced democracy in the world the cost of our elections is costing us the health of our democracy," he said.

He said Clinton could silence critics by stating "that from this point forward he and members of his family, staff and administration will campaign and raise money for only those candidates who have signed on as sponsors of serious campaign reform and who are pushing for expedited hearings and enactment."
He added that "all other candidates would be on their own."

If legislation to limit raising and spending funds is not forthcoming, Kirk suggested that Clinton name an independent commission to propose campaign reforms and put resulting legislation on a fast timetable for a vote on passage.
